title: Sweetening and rock groups
summary: Arrangers ice rock tracks and mics clip to horns.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: They've got a thing now called "sweetening" where they can add to it.

Yeah. Well, they get these rock groups. You know, it's like we were saying before, you put a lot of money behind some mediocre group and you can get them pretty famous. But I guess sometimes they're just too rotten so they've got to add -- they listen to the group and say, My God, My God, we've got to add something to this. So they get an arranger who will write the whole thing -- because these groups don't write that stuff out, they practice 25 days and learn six bars or something, you know. They're dedicated people but, I mean, they're dedicated like a guy who moves one grain of sand at a time, you know.

So then the arranger will write out something, just ice up the arrangement, pep it up a little bit and make it a little more musically interesting, since nobody can tell what words these guys are singing or anything else about it -- very interesting. So they're doing this sweetening thing, you put the earphones on and you can't hear what the guy next to you is playing, all you hear is -- (Humming). And the rhythm

section going on, you don't know whether your tones any good, you don't know if you're in tune, you don't know what the guy next to you is doing. And musicianship is -- whatever little may be left of it, is starting to go down the drain. You have this even in a lot of live performances with a lot of these rock groups, they put these little microphones in a hole in the mouthpiece. Now, when I got a hole in the mouthpiece, I used to get it repaired. Now they put one in there and put a microphone in there and you stand there -- I've seen rock groups, you know, four horns and all these electronic instruments, these enormous speakers, each horn has got a microphone and its own amplification system. You don't have to have any kind of tone at all. It wouldn't matter if he did because it would be so distorted you wouldn't know what it was.

So you speak of the future of musicianship, I don't think there is much musicianship involved in that kind of music. There's a competence involved, you know, a technical talent. Like a guy that puts together a Ford or something, he needs competence and a talent. But I don't think it's much more than that. You just have to know how to finger the right notes, you don't have to worry about the tone. God knows there's no expression, because even if there was, electronically you can forget about it. It's not in your control.
All of the artistry is out of it.
